questions.stem: Total internal reflection can only happen when light travels:

options.text: from a denser material towards a less dense one
options.explanation: The denser-to-less-dense direction is one of the two required conditions.

options.text: from a less dense material towards a denser one
options.explanation: In that direction the ray refracts towards the normal and some light always crosses.

options.text: along the boundary between two materials
options.explanation: The ray travels inside the first material and strikes the boundary, not along it.
A vacuum offers no boundary to reflect at.

questions.stem: For total internal reflection the incidence angle must be:

options.explanation: At the critical angle the ray still refracts along the boundary.
Below the threshold the ray escapes by refraction.
Beyond the critical angle nothing is transmitted — reflection is total.
A 90° incidence angle grazes the boundary and never enters the second material.

questions.stem: An endoscope carries light into a patient's body through optical fibres, which guide it by:

options.text: total internal reflection at every bounce
options.explanation: Each strike on the fibre's edge is beyond the critical angle, so light stays trapped inside.
Fibres guide light, not electricity.

options.text: sound echoes returning to the source
options.explanation: Endoscopes are optical, not acoustic.
Nothing reacts; the glass only guides the light.

questions.stem: A periscope is built from two right-angled prisms. The prisms turn the light by:

options.explanation: The light is not absorbed; it reflects without losing its path.

options.text: total internal reflection at each prism's back face
options.explanation: Light totally internally reflects in both prisms, turning it through right angles.

options.text: splitting it into colours at each face
options.explanation: Dispersion would blur the image; the prism reflects, not splits.

options.text: lensing it through a curved surface
options.explanation: Right-angled prisms have flat faces; no lensing happens.

questions.stem: Beyond the critical angle, the light that would have refracted is:

options.explanation: No energy is absorbed; reflection is total.
Transmission drops to zero, not to a dimmer ray.
Past the threshold the boundary reflects everything, obeying the reflection law.
Dispersion is a refraction effect; here refraction has stopped.

questions.stem: Name the two conditions required for total internal reflection.
questions.modelAnswer: The incidence angle must be greater than the critical angle, and the material the light starts in must be denser than the material beyond the boundary.

questions.stem: List three uses of total internal reflection named in this lesson.
questions.modelAnswer: Communications along optical fibres, endoscopes and periscopes — also acceptable: decorative lamps, binoculars, telescopes, cameras and safety reflectors.

questions.stem: Explain why light can travel along an optical fibre even when the fibre curves.
questions.modelAnswer: Each time the ray reaches the fibre's edge it strikes beyond the critical angle, so it totally internally reflects back into the glass; repeating at every bounce keeps the light trapped inside the fibre along the whole curved path.

questions.stem: A bicycle reflector returns headlight glow to the driver behind it. Explain the role of prismatic total internal reflection.
questions.modelAnswer: Light from the headlights enters the reflector's prisms, strikes their faces beyond the critical angle and totally internally reflects, so the light is turned back towards the driver instead of scattering away.

questions.stem: At the critical angle the refracted ray travels:

options.text: along the boundary at exactly 90° to the normal
options.explanation: That skim-along-the-boundary ray is the definition of the critical angle.
Retro-reflection is not what defines the critical angle.

options.text: into the second material at 45° to the normal
options.explanation: 45° is just an ordinary refraction angle, not the defining one.
Light never stops; it refracts or reflects.

questions.stem: Increasing the incidence angle from small values makes the refraction angle:

options.explanation: Both angles grow together towards the critical threshold.
The refraction angle climbs until it lies along the boundary at 90°.

options.text: stay fixed at its starting value
options.explanation: Refraction responds to every change in incidence.

options.text: reverse to the other side of the normal
options.explanation: The refracted ray stays on the far side of the normal until reflection replaces it.

questions.stem: Just past the critical angle the boundary behaves like a:

options.explanation: Nothing is absorbed — reflection is total.
No focusing happens at a flat boundary.
Beyond the critical angle the boundary reflects the ray completely, like a mirror.

options.text: prism that splits the ray into colours
options.explanation: Splitting needs refraction; past the critical angle refraction has stopped.

questions.stem: A ray inside glass heads towards air and meets the boundary exactly at the critical angle. The angle of refraction is:

options.explanation: 25° is an ordinary refraction angle, not the boundary-skimming one.
The defining angle is 90°, not 45°.
Refraction angles stop growing at 90°, and the critical angle is where they arrive there.
At the critical angle the refracted ray skims along the boundary at exactly 90° to the normal.

questions.stem: A glass-liquid boundary first shows total internal reflection when the incidence angle inside the glass reaches 65°. At an incidence angle of 70° the ray:

options.text: refracts into the liquid away from the normal
options.explanation: Refraction has already stopped — 70° is beyond the 65° threshold.

options.text: totally internally reflects inside the glass
options.explanation: Any incidence angle beyond the 65° critical angle reflects totally.
That happens exactly at 65°, not at 70°.
The reflected ray obeys the reflection law, matching the 70° incidence angle.

questions.stem: Define the critical angle.
questions.modelAnswer: The incidence angle at which the angle of refraction is exactly 90°, so the refracted ray skims along the boundary.

questions.stem: State what happens to a ray whose incidence angle is exactly the critical angle, and to one whose angle is just beyond it.
questions.modelAnswer: At the critical angle the ray refracts along the boundary at 90°; just beyond it the ray is totally internally reflected inside the denser material.

questions.stem: Explain why total internal reflection can never occur for a ray travelling from air into glass.
questions.modelAnswer: The ray would be going from a less dense material to a denser one, so refraction bends the ray towards the normal and some light always crosses the boundary; the denser-to-less-dense condition for total internal reflection is never met.

questions.stem: A glass-liquid boundary shows its first total internal reflection when the incidence angle inside the glass is 65°. State the critical angle for the boundary and the angle the reflected ray makes with the normal.
questions.modelAnswer: First total internal reflection means the lowest angle at which it occurs, so the critical angle is 65°, and the reflected ray leaves at 65° on the other side of the normal.

questions.stem: The relationship between the critical angle c and the refractive index n is:

options.explanation: The critical angle's sine is the reciprocal of the refractive index.
That would make sin c exceed 1 for every material — impossible.
The reciprocal applies to the sine of the angle, not the angle itself.
Same inversion error on the other side.

questions.stem: For a material of refractive index 2.0, sin c equals:

options.explanation: That is 1 divided by 5, not by 2.
A sine can never exceed 1.
sin c = 1 only for n = 1, the vacuum itself.

questions.stem: As a material's refractive index gets larger, its critical angle:

options.explanation: sin c = 1 / n shrinks as n grows, so c shrinks too.
The reciprocal law runs the opposite way.
The two quantities are tightly linked, not independent.
The equation stays defined for every n above 1.

questions.stem: Rearranging sin c = 1 / n gives the refractive index as:

options.explanation: That drops the reciprocal entirely.
Subtracting is not the inverse of dividing.
Invert both sides: n = 1 / sin c.
The reciprocal applies to sin c, not to the angle c.

questions.stem: Diamond sparkles more than opal mainly because diamond's:

options.explanation: The higher index gives a smaller, not larger, critical angle.
Diamond's index is the larger one, about 2.4 against opal's 1.5.
The sparkle comes from internal reflection, not surface texture.

options.text: critical angle is smaller, so total internal reflection happens over a wider range of angles
options.explanation: With c about 25° against opal's 42°, rays reflect totally across 25°-90°, bouncing more and sparkling more.

questions.stem: State the equation linking the critical angle to the refractive index.
questions.modelAnswer: sin c = 1 / n, where c is the critical angle and n is the refractive index.

questions.stem: For diamond, refractive index 2.4, state sin c and the critical angle.
questions.modelAnswer: sin c = 1 / 2.4 = 0.417, so c = sin⁻¹(0.417) = 24.6°, which rounds to 25°.

questions.stem: Explain why a ray of light inside a diamond is more likely to be totally internally reflected than one inside glass.
questions.modelAnswer: Diamond's refractive index is higher, so by sin c = 1 / n its critical angle is smaller; incidence angles exceed that smaller critical angle over a wider range, so total internal reflection happens more often inside the diamond.

questions.stem: Opal has refractive index about 1.5 and diamond about 2.4. Calculate both critical angles and explain which stone appears to sparkle more.
questions.modelAnswer: For opal sin c = 1 / 1.5 = 0.667, so c = 41.8°, about 42°; for diamond sin c = 1 / 2.4 = 0.417, so c = 24.6°, about 25°. Diamond's smaller critical angle means total internal reflection occurs across the wider 25° to 90° range, so more light bounces inside and diamond sparkles more.
